To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ranked-set sample estimators of probability densities are generally more accurate and efficient than their simple random sample counterparts.

the kernel density estimator based on ranked-set samples is unbiased and consistent for any probability density function, and that it is asymptotically more efficient than the estimator based on a random sample of the same size.

(a) the kernel density estimator based on ranked set sampling (RSS) is asymptotically normal with the usual variance formula; (b) the RSS kernel density estimator has smaller bias and mean squared error (MSE) than its simple random sample (SRS) counterpart for most densities and for small samples; (c) for large samples, the MSE of the RSS kernel density estimate is smaller than the MSE of the SRS kernel density estimate for all densities except for the normal distribution;

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ranked-set sample estimators are superior to the usual estimators for most of the cases.
, for the models considered, the ranked-set kernel estimators have better small-sample properties, but the usual kernel estimators have smaller mean squared errors for large samples.
the ranked-set estimators perform as well as or better than the corresponding simple random sample estimator for the same number of observations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ranked-set sample estimators are superior to the random sample estimators in the sense of having a smaller mean square error.
the ranked-set kernel estimators can be more efficient than their simple random sample counterparts in terms of integrated mean squared error.
the use of ranked-set samples in kernel estimation can improve the performance of density estimators in many situations.
